title: Buffers in Node.js
idea: A Buffer is a fixed-size block of raw bytes. Node uses it for data that is not text yet, such as file contents, network data and images.

analogy.text: A row of numbered boxes, each holding one number from 0 to 255. What the numbers mean depends on how you read them.
analogy.breaks: Unlike boxes, a buffer cannot grow; copy it into a bigger one.

points: An encoding such as UTF-8 maps characters to bytes and back.
One character takes one to four bytes, so counts differ.
A file read without an encoding returns a Buffer, as does network data.
A Buffer has a fixed size and is indexed from 0, like an array.

parts.label: 1 byte
parts.note: Plain English letters and digits use one byte. `A` is byte `41`, written in hex (base 16).

parts.label: 2 bytes
parts.note: Many accented letters use two bytes. `é` is `c3 a9`.

parts.label: 3 bytes
parts.note: Many symbols use three bytes. `€` is `e2 82 ac`.

code.title: Characters vs bytes
code.caption: Compare the two counts, then change `€` to `e` in `text` and run again.

code.title: Bytes that are not text
code.caption: Not every byte sequence is valid UTF-8 text. Watch what the string step does to the first byte.

pitfalls: Do not use a string's `.length` as its size in bytes; use `Buffer.byteLength`.
Keep binary data as a Buffer; a UTF-8 string round trip can corrupt it.
Buffers cannot grow; join them into a new one with `Buffer.concat` (next page).

quiz.why: `'€'.length` counts one character. UTF-8 stores € in three bytes (`e2 82 ac`), so the buffer length is 3.

takeaway: A Buffer is bytes; text is bytes plus an encoding.

starters: Is a Buffer the same as a Uint8Array?
